summary: This RFC describes a Flexible Cross-Connect service for EVPN-VPWS, a way to carry point-to-point Ethernet circuits across a provider network. It lets many attachment circuits from different Ethernet Segments and physical interfaces share a single service tunnel, while still supporting Single-Active and All-Active multihoming.

eli5.summary: A shipping company puts many small parcels from different trucks into one big container. This does that for network connections, saving tunnels while keeping backup paths working.

subtitle: How a provider can squeeze huge numbers of VLAN circuits into one EVPN tunnel without losing backup paths.

tldr.problem: Service providers have millions of attachment circuits to backhaul, and signaling one VPWS service tunnel and one set of BGP routes per circuit (as RFC 8214 does) costs too many labels, too much OAM monitoring and too much BGP signaling.
tldr.mechanism: Flexible Cross-Connect rewrites VLAN IDs into unique 'normalized' VIDs and multiplexes many circuits from several Ethernet Segments into one EVPN-VPWS service tunnel, in either a default mode with no per-VLAN signaling or a VLAN-signaled mode with one route per normalized VID.
tldr.outcome: Providers keep Single-Active and All-Active multi-homing and fast convergence while using far fewer service tunnels. The catch is that both ends must do VLAN tag manipulation and a second VID lookup.

today: RFC 9744 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 8214 and RFC 7432.

sections.title: Why Flexible Cross-Connect Exists
sections.content:
RFC 8214 delivers point-to-point services over BGP using the constructs of RFC 7432. Each service runs between a pair of Attachment Circuits (ACs), where an AC on a Provider Edge (PE) router can be a port, a VLAN on a port, or a group of VLANs on a port. It also brings multi-homing (Single-Active and All-Active) and fast convergence.

Service providers have a very large number of ACs, in the millions, to backhaul across an MPLS/IP network. They want to multiplex many of them, across several physical interfaces on one or more PEs, onto a single VPWS service tunnel. That reduces the number of EVPN service labels and the OAM monitoring tied to them, and it reduces EVPN BGP signaling. They want this without losing the capabilities of RFC 8214.

This document, called the EVPN-VPWS Flexible Cross-Connect (FXC) service, extends EVPN-VPWS to do that. A thorough understanding of RFC 7432 and RFC 8214 is a prerequisite.
sections.eli5: A big phone company has millions of little wires to carry. Giving every wire its own tunnel is too much work, so this lets many wires share one tunnel.

sections.title: The Multi-homing Problem
sections.content:
In RFC 8214 a PE signals an AC indirectly. It ties the AC to a VPWS service tunnel and advertises that tunnel in an Ethernet A-D per EVI route, with the Ethernet Tag field set to a 24-bit VPWS service instance identifier and the ESI field set to the 10-octet identifier of the Ethernet Segment (ES). Remote PEs can therefore tie each tunnel to a remote ES, and a 'mass withdrawal' when that ES fails lets them update their next-hop adjacency list quickly.

If many ACs from various ESs share one tunnel and are not signaled in BGP, remote PEs cannot relate the remote ES, the remote ACs and the tunnel. When the ES fails they cannot redirect traffic to another multi-homing PE.

The RFC gives two answers. For single-homed endpoints, not signaling each AC is acceptable because no alternative path exists; the cost is that traffic for a failed AC crosses the core and is discarded at the destination PE. For multi-homed endpoints there are two options: signal each AC via BGP (the VLAN-signaled FXC), or bundle several ACs on an ES per destination endpoint and tie the bundle to one tunnel.
sections.eli5: If everyone's mail goes in one big box and nobody writes down who is inside, then when one street is closed nobody knows which mail to reroute. So there are two fixes: list everyone, or bundle mail by destination.

sections.title: Normalized VIDs and the Two Lookups
sections.content:
Several physical interfaces can use the same VLAN IDs, so FXC translates VIDs into unique ones, called a normalized VID. If more than 4095 VLANs are multiplexed onto one tunnel, a single tag to double tag translation is required.

With a single normalized VID, the lower 12 bits of the Ethernet Tag ID field MUST be set to that VID. With a double normalized VID, the lower 12 bits MUST carry the inner VID and the higher 12 bits are set to the outer VID. 24-bit VPWS service instance identifiers and 12-bit identifiers for normalized VIDs MUST be right-aligned.

Because one tunnel now serves many interfaces, an MPLS label lookup alone cannot pick the egress interface. At the disposition PE the EVPN label lookup identifies a VID-VRF, and a lookup of the normalized VID in that table identifies the egress endpoint. VID normalization MUST be completed before MPLS encapsulation on the ingress PE, so both PEs must be able to rewrite, add or delete VLAN tags. The RFC warns operators about performance trade-offs compared with typical pseudowire processing.

The Ethernet Tag ID value may represent a unique value for a group of VLANs (VLAN Bundle Service Interface) or a unique value for an individual VLAN, equal to the normalized VID (VLAN-Aware Bundle Service Interface).
sections.eli5: Two schools may both have a 'Room 5'. So each room gets a new unique number first. At the other end, the mail clerk reads the room number on the parcel to know where to deliver it.

sections.title: Default FXC Mode
sections.content:
In the default mode, many ACs across several ESs share one EVPN-VPWS service tunnel represented by a single VPWS service ID. The PEs do not signal the VLANs (normalized VIDs) in BGP, so both PEs MUST know the VLANs through configuration. There should ideally be a single point-to-point tunnel between a pair of PEs for a given set of ACs.

The PE sends an Ethernet A-D per-EVI route with an ESI of 0, the Ethernet Tag set to a VPWS service instance ID, and the MPLS label set to a dynamically generated EVPN service label. The Route Target representing the EVI can be auto-generated per Section 5.1.2.1 of RFC 8365. The route also carries the EVPN Layer 2 Attributes Extended Community with two new flags. The receiver uses them for a consistency check and MAY raise an alarm, but it will not disrupt the service.

Only one route is sent, when the first AC with a normalized VID is configured. Later ACs are associated locally and trigger no further BGP routes.

The mode can also be used for multi-homing. A group of normalized VIDs for ACs on a single ES, all destined to one endpoint, is multiplexed into one tunnel. There can then be several tunnels per pair of PEs, one for each group of VIDs.
sections.eli5: All the parcels go into one container with one label on it. The sender announces the container only once, and the people at each end just know from their own lists which parcels are inside.

sections.title: VLAN-Signaled FXC and Local Switching
sections.content:
In the VLAN-signaled mode, many normalized VIDs across several ESs still share one tunnel, but that tunnel is represented by multiple VPWS service IDs, one per normalized VID, and they are signaled in BGP. For each normalized VID on each ES, the PE generates an Ethernet A-D per-EVI route whose ESI is the ES, whose Ethernet Tag is the normalized VID, and whose MPLS label is the same tunnel label for all ACs on that tunnel.

Because VIDs are signaled, a PE can cross-check them. If the same normalized VID is configured on three PEs for one EVI, a PE receiving the second remote route generates an error unless both routes have the same ESI. The default mode cannot do this.

When two ACs on two multi-homed ESs sit on the same set of multi-homing PEs, traffic MUST be switched locally during normal operation. A PE receiving an Ethernet A-D per-EVI route with a local ESI does not change its forwarding state, so local switching takes precedence. In that case the route should carry an MPLS label tied to the destination AC or ES, since the same normalized VID can be reachable via two ESs.
sections.eli5: Here the sender writes every parcel's room number on a public board so mistakes can be spotted. And if both rooms are in the same building, the parcel is carried down the hall instead of going out through the post office.

sections.title: The Extended Community Flags
sections.content:
FXC reuses the EVPN Layer 2 Attributes Extended Community from RFC 8214 and adds two fields, M and V, to its Control Flags. The community is sent with the Ethernet A-D per-EVI route and SHOULD be sent for both Single-Active and All-Active redundancy modes. Remaining bits MUST be zero when sending and ignored when receiving.

M gives the mode: 00 as defined in RFC 8214, 01 VLAN-signaled FXC, 10 default FXC. V gives the VID normalization: 00 per RFC 8214, 01 single-VID, 10 double-VID. Both fields are OPTIONAL, and M is ignored at reception for forwarding purposes and used for error notifications.

If V is sent and the endpoints disagree, for example one in single-tag mode and the other in double-tag mode, the tunnel must not be established. If single VID normalization is signaled (12 bits) but the data plane uses double tags, normalization applies only to the outer tag. For IANA, bits 8-11 of the EVPN Layer 2 Attributes Control Flags registry were allocated: M is bits 10-11 and V is bits 8-9.
sections.eli5: Two small stickers are added to the container's label. One says how the parcels are listed, and the other says how the room numbers are written, so both ends can check they agree.

sections.title: Failure Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC walks through two topologies: default FXC (Figure 1) and VLAN-signaled FXC (Figure 2). Failure of an EVPN-VPWS service can be detected by OAM such as BFD for pseudowire VCCV, and then the switch over to the backup PE follows the procedures above.

  • Attachment circuit failure: in default FXC the failure is not signaled, so a remote PE may keep sending traffic to the failed AC and it is lost at the egress PE; application layer OAM may be used. In VLAN-signaled FXC the Ethernet A-D per-EVI route for that normalized VID is withdrawn and the remote PE removes the failing PE from its adjacency list.
  • PE port failure: in default FXC the route for the affected service tunnel is withdrawn. In VLAN-signaled FXC the per-EVI routes for the normalized VIDs are withdrawn along with the Ethernet A-D per-ES route. Either way the remote PE removes the failing PE from its adjacency list.
  • PE node failure: similar, except the route reflector performs the withdrawals instead of the PE.
sections.eli5: If one road is blocked, the VLAN-signaled mode tells everyone right away which road. In the default mode nobody is told about a single blocked lane, but a whole closed highway is announced.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC treats FXC as a multiplexing capability that rides on existing EVPN-VPWS signaling. Since no functionality beyond that muxing is added, it states that no additional security considerations are needed beyond those already specified in RFC 8214.
sections.eli5: Nothing new that could be attacked was added, so the existing safety rules still cover it.
